channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Moody's has downgraded Poland's credit rating to A3, the first downgrade of the country in 24 years, with Polish 10-year bond yields above 6% for several weeks, according to Les Echos.
item.description:
Les Echos reports that the 2027 budget will show a deficit above 6% of GDP for the third consecutive year. Most of the measures planned by Donald Tusk's government to balance public finances have been vetoed by the President, and even if implemented they would account for only about 10% of the effort needed to reduce the deficit, according to the report. The next elections, at the end of 2027, are described as undecided and as not favouring an austerity programme. The reporting does not give Moody's stated rationale or outlook, the rating from which Poland was downgraded, or the positions of the other rating agencies. It does not give the level of public debt against GDP, and it does not say how the zloty or Polish equities reacted. The 6% yield is given as a level held over weeks, not as a move on the day of the downgrade.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Poland is one of the larger manufacturing locations in Central Europe, which is background rather than something the report states. A downgrade combined with 10-year yields above 6% on a general reading raises the cost of borrowing for the state and tends to feed through to corporate and project financing in the same market. On the same general reading, the fiscal constraint may also limit the room for public investment and support measures in the construction and infrastructure markets. The immediate effect on demand is not measured in the reporting. Points that may be worth considering include how Polish customer financing conditions evolve, whether public investment programmes are affected by the deficit constraint, and how currency exposure to the zloty is being managed.

Les Echos

item.title: The EU has agreed to remove sanctions on Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, which Bloomberg reports will allow sanctions on nearly 3,000 people and companies to be prolonged for three years rather than renewed every six months.
item.description:
France had requested Usmanov's removal and Luxembourg Fridman's, according to Il Sole 24 Ore, and Bloomberg attributes the three-year prolongation to the rotating EU presidency, held by Ireland. Der Standard reports that three member states wanted the two exempted while Latvia opposed it, and that without an agreement the sanctions would have expired. Süddeutsche Zeitung describes the delisting as the price of avoiding a threatened total blockade of the Russia sanctions by individual member states. The listings cover individuals, entities and companies accused of supporting Russia's war against Ukraine or benefiting from the Kremlin's policies, with travel restrictions and asset freezes in the EU. EU High Representative Kaja Kallas said sanctions remain the cornerstone of EU policy to pressure Moscow. The link between the renewal and the two delistings comes from people familiar with the matter speaking anonymously to Bloomberg, and the reporting does not say whether the same approach applies to the EU's separate economic and sectoral sanctions.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The operational point is predictability rather than the two names. A regime renewed every six months carries a recurring risk of lapse or veto, and a three-year horizon removes that, which bears on compliance planning for any company with Russian counterparties. The reporting covers individual listings, not the sectoral measures on trade in goods, so the change does not by itself alter what may be traded. The cost of the deal — delisting under pressure from member states — shows, on a general reading, that the need for agreement among all member states continues to shape the sanctions regime. Points that may be worth considering include whether the three-year horizon extends to the sectoral packages, how screening of counterparties handles delistings, and whether other listings come under similar pressure.

Bloomberg | Der Standard | Süddeutsche Zeitung | Il Sole 24 Ore

item.title: China announced on 22 September that two drug precursor chemicals have been added to an export-control catalogue requiring licences for shipments to the US, Mexico and Canada, raising the number of listed chemicals to 18 from 16.
item.description:
The joint announcement came from the Ministry of Commerce, the Ministry of Public Security, the Ministry of Emergency Management, the General Administration of Customs and the National Medical Products Administration, according to Global Times. Chemicals in Part I of the annex need licences for export to the US, Mexico and Canada, and those in Part II for export to Myanmar, Laos and Afghanistan. The change was rolled out before the Washington summit between Xi Jinping and Donald Trump. The Trump administration has repeatedly called on Beijing to do more to stem the flow of precursor chemicals used to make fentanyl, and China is the primary origin of those precursors, according to The Straits Times. None of the reports names the two chemicals, their industrial uses, or the volumes traded. The reporting does not say how long licence applications take, whether existing contracts are affected, or whether the addition is linked to any US tariff measure.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

A licence requirement changes the terms on which a chemical crosses a border even when the volume is small: on a general reading, shipments can continue, but on a timetable set by the exporting authority. Without the names of the two substances, the direct relevance to any industrial supply chain cannot be judged from this reporting. The wider reading is that chemical export controls remain an instrument China uses in its relationship with the US, placed here before a summit. Points that may be worth considering include whether either substance has industrial uses in North American supply chains, whether the licensing regime becomes part of summit outcomes, and how further additions to the list would be monitored.

Global Times | MarketScreener | The Straits Times

item.title: Cox Automotive figures show US electric vehicle sales fell by nearly 24% year on year in the first six months of 2026, while second-quarter sales rose more than 14% on the first quarter as petrol prices increased.
item.description:
The federal government ended its USD 7,500 tax credit for plug-in models on 30 September 2025, and USA Today reports the first-half decline against that background. The quarter-on-quarter rise is attributed in the reporting to rising gasoline prices. So the two figures describe different comparisons: the year-on-year fall measures the loss against a period when the credit applied, and the quarterly rise measures movement within 2026 as fuel costs climbed. The reporting does not give unit volumes, the electric share of total US sales, a breakdown by manufacturer, or any figure for the third quarter to date. It does not separate pure electric from plug-in hybrid sales. It also does not say whether the second-quarter rise came from existing buyers pulling purchases forward, from new model launches, or from price cuts, and gives no forecast for the rest of the year.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The first-half fall coincides with a policy change a year ago; the quarterly rise reflects fuel prices now, and the two point in different directions. Rising gasoline prices, which the reporting links to the second-quarter rise, sit alongside the record diesel prices in today's diesel brief, so on a general reading electric-vehicle demand in the US has become partly an energy-price story rather than only a subsidy story. For suppliers to battery and electric-drive assembly the volume signal is mixed, and the absence of unit figures limits how far it can be used. Points that may be worth considering include how North American battery and electric-drive programmes have adjusted since the credit ended, whether the second-quarter rise continued into the third, and how US demand trends compare with the shifting Spanish production mix reported today.

USA Today

item.title: President Macron has asked the European Commission for flexibility to strengthen import and short-term production capacity for petroleum products, and urged it to postpone new methane reporting rules for oil and gas importers.
item.description:
The methane letter is dated 18 September. On refined products, TF1 Info reports that the constraint today is less the availability of crude than of refined products, whose transport and processing are affected by Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, Iranian strikes in the Middle East and the blockade of the Straits of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb. France imports over 99% of its crude and, on Enerdata figures, imported 47% of the diesel and 21% of the gasoline it consumed in 2025. On methane, the EU rules due to take effect on 1 January require monitoring and verification of methane emissions for oil and gas deliveries to the bloc, with fines for breaches. Macron's letter, first reported by Les Echos and seen by Reuters, argues the rules could create legal risk for importers as energy supplies tighten. Reuters reporting carried by MarketScreener sets the letter against pressure from unions and opposition parties over the cost of living ahead of the 2027 presidential election. The reporting does not describe what "flexibility" would mean in legal terms, whether other member states support either request, or how the Commission has responded.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The two requests point the same way: loosening constraints on how oil, gas and refined products reach Europe while supply is short. The reporting identifies the availability of refined products, rather than crude, as the constraint, and for a manufacturer the relevant products are diesel for logistics and the refinery streams that feed petrochemical chains; the second link is a general reading rather than something the reports state. A postponed methane regime would ease compliance for importers but would also delay monitoring and verification requirements, backed by fines, on oil and gas deliveries to the EU. Both are requests from one member state, not decisions. Points that may be worth considering include whether other member states join either request, whether the Commission responds before the 1 January start of the methane rules, and how European refined-product supply is reflected in current energy and freight assumptions.

TF1 Info | MarketScreener

item.title: Anfac, the Spanish car and truck manufacturers' association, reports that car production in Spain fell 1.8% in January to August 2026 to 1.4 million units, while vehicle exports fell 2.8% to 1,235,865 units.
item.description:
Within the total, production of pure electric vehicles rose 28.8% to 88,842 units, plug-in hybrids fell 13.5%, and hybrids grew 18.4% to 462,696 units. La Vanguardia reports that new electrified models entering production allowed a slight improvement in the last two months, and that growth in electrified and hybrid output compensated for the decline in exports. Europe remains the dominant destination, at 90.8% of shipments in July and 89% in August, slightly lower than a year earlier by 0.3 and 1.2 percentage points respectively, which El Correo attributes to lower demand from several EU and other European partners. El Correo reports the evolution of production as within manufacturers' forecasts, in line with a year-end estimate of around 2.25 million vehicles manufactured. The reporting does not break production down by manufacturer or plant, does not give a monthly path beyond the remark on the last two months, and does not separate passenger cars from commercial vehicles in the export figure.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Spain is Europe's second-largest vehicle producer, which is background rather than something the reports state, and its output here is broadly flat with a changing mix. The mix is the part that bears on materials: pure electric and hybrid output rising while plug-in hybrids and exports fall means what Spanish plants build is shifting even as the total barely moves, and drivetrain changes affect bonding, sealing and thermal-management content — a general reading rather than something Anfac addresses. The declining European share of exports points to weaker demand in the main destination markets. Points that may be worth considering include how Spanish plant supply is weighted between electrified and combustion programmes, whether the last-two-months improvement carries into the autumn, and how the export weakness compares with demand trends in the main European destinations.

La Vanguardia | El Correo

item.title: IG Metall's regional bargaining commissions adopted a 5% wage demand for the metal and electrical industry on 22 September, with the executive board due to approve it on 23 September and negotiations with employers beginning in early October.
item.description:
The Süddeutsche Zeitung describes the demand as restrained by the union's standards: IG Metall demanded 8% for one year for the whole industry in 2022 and 7% in 2024. The paper attributes the lower figure to the pressure on large parts of German industry, naming the automotive sector and mechanical engineering. It also notes that the union always sets its opening demand relatively high, in the knowledge that the settlement will be significantly lower. The two reports give different sizes for the workforce covered — the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung and the Süddeutsche Zeitung do not agree — so the figure is left out here; both describe millions of employees. The reporting does not give a contract duration for the 5% demand, does not say whether it includes any one-off payments or working-time elements, and gives no employer response. It does not say which regional bargaining area is expected to set the pattern.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The metal and electrical industry covers the automotive, machinery and electrical-equipment customers that make up much of German industrial demand, so the round sets labour costs across a large part of the domestic customer base, though, on a general reading, not in the chemical industry itself, which bargains separately. A demand below the last two rounds, from a union that openly pitches high, points to a settlement shaped by the same cost pressure that appears in the Mercedes statement reported today. No settlement date is reported, and the demand is an opening position, not a result. Points that may be worth considering include how German customers' cost programmes might respond to the eventual settlement, whether the round extends to working-time terms, and how the outcome compares with the chemical industry's own agreements.

Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | Süddeutsche Zeitung

item.title: Mercedes-Benz production director Michael Schiebe told a works meeting on 21 September that if costs in Germany do not fall, the company will have to close one German assembly plant and one German powertrain plant.
item.description:
The meeting was held in Sindelfingen, and a company spokesman confirmed the statements to dpa. They were first reported by the Stuttgarter Zeitung and Stuttgarter Nachrichten. Each of Mercedes' three German assembly plants can currently build around 300,000 cars, so together Mercedes produces around 900,000 units in Germany, according to the Frankfurter Rundschau. The statement is conditional: it names the consequence of costs not falling rather than announcing a closure, and it does not name which assembly plant or which powertrain plant would be affected. The reporting does not set a deadline by which costs must fall, does not quantify the cost gap management wants closed, and does not say whether the measure would mean moving output abroad or reducing total output. It gives no response from the works council or from IG Metall to this specific statement. The context in the same reporting is limited to the plant capacities; it does not tie the statement to IG Metall's wage demand, reported separately.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Closing one of three assembly plants would, on the reported figures, remove about 300,000 units, roughly a third of Mercedes' German output, if the output were not moved elsewhere in Germany. A powertrain plant is the other half of the statement, and powertrain and assembly consume different materials — sealing and bonding in drivetrains on one side, body and interior bonding on the other — which is a general reading rather than something the reporting addresses. The statement is a conditional management position, not a decision, and it names no site. Points that may be worth considering include which German Mercedes sites are supplied from which locations, whether management sets a timetable for the cost reductions, and how German automotive volume assumptions for the coming planning period hold up against a possible loss of a third of one manufacturer's German assembly capacity.

Frankfurter Rundschau

item.title: Taiwan's Ministry of Economic Affairs reported on 22 September that export orders reached USD 103 billion in August 2026, up 71.4% year on year and the first month above USD 100 billion, with electronics orders up 83.9%.
item.description:
By destination, orders from the United States rose 88.9% and from Europe 58.2%. Handelsblatt gives China at 47.7% and MarketScreener gives Japan at 41.1%; the two outlets list different third markets. By product, electronic products rose 83.9%, and MarketScreener gives telecoms products at 100.5%. The reporting does not give the month-on-month change, the ministry's outlook for the coming months, or the split between orders produced in Taiwan and those fulfilled at overseas plants. It also does not separate price from volume, so how much of the 71.4% reflects higher unit values of advanced components rather than more units is not visible.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Electronics assembly is a large end-market for adhesives, encapsulants and thermal-interface materials, and Taiwanese orders sit near the top of that supply chain; the link is a general reading rather than something the ministry states. Orders growing faster from the US and Europe than from China indicate where demand for Taiwanese electronics is coming from. On a general reading, orders precede shipments, so the figure bears on demand in the months ahead rather than today. The absence of a price and volume split limits how far it can be read as unit growth. Points that may be worth considering include whether electronics customers in the region are adjusting material forecasts to the order level, how much of the growth sits in telecoms and other electronic products, and whether the pattern continues in the September figure.

MarketScreener | Handelsblatt

item.title: India has amended the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011, requiring packages of soaps, shampoos, toothpastes, other cosmetics and toiletries to display a green dot for vegetarian origin or a red or brown dot for non-vegetarian origin.
item.description:
The change is made by the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Fourth Amendment Rules, 2026. The symbol must appear at the top of the principal display panel of the package, so that consumers can identify the product's origin at a glance. The reporting does not give a date from which the rule applies, a transition period for existing stock and printed packaging, or the definition of "non-vegetarian origin" — in particular whether it covers only active ingredients or also processing aids and other components. It does not say how compliance will be checked or what penalties apply, and it gives no estimate of how many products or brands are affected. It also does not say whether imported products are covered on the same terms as domestically produced ones.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

A mandatory symbol in a fixed position on the main panel is a packaging-design change for every affected product sold in India, and, on a general reading, label and pack redesigns tend to move through printing, labelling and converting at the same time. For the materials side the less visible question is the definition: if origin is assessed across all components rather than the formulation alone, suppliers of ingredients and processing materials could be asked to document the origin of what they supply — the reporting does not say whether this applies. Points that may be worth considering include when the rule takes effect and how long the transition runs, how "origin" is defined for components and processing aids, and whether customers in personal care are already asking suppliers for origin declarations.

Business Standard | LiveMint

item.title: President Trump said on 22 September that he supports the idea of a ban on US diesel exports, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the administration is examining whether a partial or full ban would work and is feasible.
item.description:
The statement came as Republican lawmakers from farm states and rural regions, led by Iowa senator Chuck Grassley, were calling for action on diesel prices; the Financial Times reports it came after Trump's meeting with Ukraine's President Zelenskyy in New York. US diesel reached a record USD 6.53 a gallon on 22 September, according to the FT, which puts the rise since the Iran war began in late February at more than 70%. European diesel futures closed at an all-time high the previous week, more than double their level at the start of 2026. The supply picture behind this: the wars in Iran and Ukraine have cut exports from producers including Russia, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, disruption has spread to the Red Sea, where Saudi Arabia loads most of its diesel, and Kpler data show Middle East diesel exports halved from March to August against a year earlier, to an average of 800,000 barrels a day. The Middle East supplied nearly 41% of Europe's diesel imports in 2025. The US exported a record 1.6 million barrels a day of diesel in August, up from about 1 million in February. Commercial Times links the move to the November midterm elections. The reporting gives no timetable, no legal instrument and no indication of which destinations a partial ban would cover.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The US has become a larger diesel supplier to the rest of the world during the war, so a US ban would remove volume from a market where the Middle East, which supplied nearly 41% of Europe's diesel imports in 2025, has halved its diesel exports. Diesel is the fuel under road freight and much industrial logistics, so the effect would reach inbound raw material movements and outbound distribution alike rather than any single product line. The decision is not taken: the President has backed an idea and the Treasury is testing feasibility, so what is measurable today is the price level and the export volume at risk. Points that may be worth considering include how diesel and freight surcharges are handled in current European logistics contracts, whether a partial ban would be targeted by destination, and how exposed European distribution is to US-origin diesel.

Financial Times | The Globe and Mail | MarketScreener | Commercial Times | The Economic Times | Daily Sabah

item.title: The new VDI Guideline 4095 E, "Assessment of Plastics in the Circular Economy", consolidates key terms, legal frameworks, recycling processes and evaluation methods for plastics, aiming to make high-quality recycled materials easier to use in Germany.
item.description:
The guideline's stated purpose is to establish a common language for all stakeholders along the value chain. Its declared goals are to make high-quality recyclates easier to use, to increase planning and investment certainty, and to accelerate the transition from individual pilot projects to an industrially established circular economy. The reporting does not say which evaluation methods the guideline adopts, whether it sets any thresholds or grades for recyclate quality, how it treats multi-material products, or whether it addresses the removal or compatibility of joining and bonding materials during recycling. It gives no date for application and does not say how the guideline relates to the EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation, or whether it is a draft or a final version. It is a German guideline, and the reporting gives no indication of uptake outside Germany.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

A shared vocabulary for assessing recyclability matters to adhesive technologies because, on a general reading, bonded and laminated products are where definitions of "recyclable" and "high-quality recyclate" are most likely to be contested. On a general reading rather than anything in the source, guidelines of this kind tend to become the reference that customers, auditors and procurement teams quote, even without legal force, and so shape which material combinations are treated as compatible with recycling. The reporting does not describe the guideline as binding, so its effect depends on who adopts it. Points that may be worth considering include how the guideline's evaluation methods treat bonding layers and other joining materials, whether German customers in packaging and consumer goods plan to reference it in specifications, and how its terms line up with the definitions used under the EU packaging regulation.

ChemEurope
